subject: Sampling distributions, standard error and confidence intervals: how much a statistic varies from sample to sample, and how to turn one sample into a range of plausible values
outOfScope: Hypothesis tests, p-values and significance levels (the next pack); this pack only notes that values outside an interval are not plausible estimates
Confidence intervals for a difference between two groups, and comparing groups, beyond naming them (see the A/B testing pack); paired designs
Sample-size and power calculations, such as choosing n for a target margin of error (see the A/B testing pack)
Bayesian credible intervals and probability statements about a parameter (see the Bayesian inference pack)
Survey design and the sources of bias in depth: frames, non-response, question wording and weighting (see the Sampling and surveys pack)
Probability distributions themselves: the normal and binomial distributions, their tables and probabilities (see the Probability distributions pack)
Describing data with a mean, a standard deviation and the empirical rule (see the Descriptive statistics pack)
Intervals for a variance or standard deviation, a regression slope or a correlation, and exact or Wilson intervals for a proportion in detail
Derivations and proofs, such as those behind the t distribution and the central limit theorem
Finite population corrections when sampling without replacement from a small population
Tooling: Excel, R, Python, Minitab, StatKey and BI tools

concepts.title: Bootstrapping: resampling the sample
concepts.outcome: Describe how a bootstrap distribution is built by resampling one sample with replacement, and why it approximates the sampling distribution.

keyPoints.text: Bootstrapping is a resampling procedure that uses the data from one sample to generate a sampling distribution, by repeatedly taking random samples from that sample.

anchor.start: Bootstrapping is a resampling procedure that

keyPoints.text: Resampling is done with replacement, putting each case back after it is drawn, so a case can appear in a bootstrap sample more than once. The distribution of many bootstrapped sample means is the bootstrap distribution.

keyPoints.text: Theory shows that bootstrap proportions vary around the sample proportion much as sample proportions vary around the true parameter, so the bootstrap values can produce an interval estimate for the parameter.

keyPoints.text: Taking repeated samples from the population makes no sense, because one larger sample would serve you better. Bootstrapping instead measures how samples behave under an estimate of the population.

misconceptions.claim: Bootstrapping solves the problem of a small sample by creating more data.
misconceptions.correction: Bootstrapping is not a method for navigating small samples. Like methods built on mathematical models, it works best when a large random sample has been taken; it captures a statistic's variability when the mathematical model is unknown.

concepts.outcome: Explain that a confidence interval measures only sampling variability, so a biased sample can miss the truth however narrow its interval. (Sources of bias are taught in the Sampling and surveys pack.)
